title: How Distressed Are Consumers? Reconciling Diverging Credit Card Delinquency Measures - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed researchers argue the alarming rise in the credit card 'stock' 90+ day delinquency rate (7.6% in 2022:Q3 to 12.8% in 2026:Q1) is a measurement artifact: it is driven almost entirely by charged-off 'severely derogatory' balances that lenders now report to credit bureaus for far longer (80% still reported after one year in 2024 versus ~40% in 2004-12). Strip those stale balances out and the CCP stock rate lines up with both the flow (new transitions) rate and the Board's Call Report 30+ day rate — all of which are elevated but flat since early 2024. Total household debt fell $13 billion in 2026:Q2, with mortgage and student loan balances down slightly.

themes.theme: The headline consumer-distress scare is a measurement artifact

insights.claim: The share of US credit card balances 90+ days delinquent rose from 7.6 percent in 2022:Q3 to 12.8 percent in 2026:Q1 — a level that has fueled comparisons to the Great Recession — but the NY Fed attributes the increase to accounting/reporting mechanics rather than deteriorating borrower behavior.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Bearish consumer-credit narratives built on the 12.8% headline are quoting a series contaminated by stale charge-offs; do not size a US consumer-stress trade off this number alone.

themes.theme: Stock vs flow vs Call Report: the measurement framework

insights.claim: The 'stock' delinquency rate is the share of outstanding balance actively reported on credit reports that is 90+ days past due, while the Board of Governors' Call Report rate is the share of outstanding balance on lenders' balance sheets that is 30+ days past due — a broader delinquency definition but a narrower balance universe.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
entities: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
insights.so_what: Reusable rule for reading any credit series: check both the delinquency threshold and which balances remain in the denominator before comparing levels across sources.
insights.quote: the Board’s delinquency rate is calculated as the share of outstanding balance on lenders’ balance sheets that is 30+ days past due

insights.claim: The flow delinquency rate is constructed as the balance on loans that became 90+ days past due in the current quarter divided by the balance of loans that were less than 90 days past due in the prior quarter, annualized using a four-quarter moving sum.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Knowing the four-quarter moving-sum annualization matters for timing: the flow series smooths and lags true quarterly turning points by construction.
insights.quote: This figure is calculated as the balance on loans that became 90+ days past due in the present quarter divided by the balance of loans that were less than 90 days past due in the previous quarter, annualized using a four-quarter moving sum.

insights.claim: The stock delinquency rate is governed by exactly three forces: the pace at which new debts become delinquent, the rate at which existing delinquent debts cure back to current, and the length of time older charged-off debts remain in the data.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: A three-factor decomposition any analyst can apply to auto, student loan or mortgage stock delinquency series to test whether a rise is inflow, cure-rate, or reporting-duration driven.
insights.quote: (1) the pace at which new debts become delinquent, which the flow rate captures; (2) the rate at which existing delinquent debts cure back to current; and (3) the length of time that older charged off debts remain in the data

insights.claim: The counterintuitive fact that the CCP 90+ day stock rate sits consistently above the Board's 30+ day rate is explained by charge-off accounting: at charge-off, typically between 120 and 180 days past due, the balance leaves lenders' books and exits both numerator and denominator, registering only once, whereas credit-bureau data keeps the still-owed debt in the stock.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Explains why bank-reported card credit metrics can look benign while bureau-based consumer distress metrics look severe — the gap is structural, not a contradiction to arbitrage.
insights.quote: when a loan is charged-off—typically between 120 and 180 days past due—the balance comes off the lenders’ books, exiting both the numerator and the denominator. The charge-off registers once, in the period it occurs, and then it is gone.

themes.theme: Lender reporting behavior has structurally changed since 2004

insights.claim: The share of borrowers' charged-off debts still being reported to credit bureaus one year later doubled from about 40 percent over 2004-2012 to 80 percent by 2024.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: This single ratio is the mechanical driver of the headline delinquency scare; any historical comparison of stock delinquency to pre-2013 levels is apples-to-oranges.
insights.quote: Between 2004 and 2012, only about 40 percent of borrowers’ charged-off debts were still being reported one year later; by 2024, this figure had doubled to 80 percent.

insights.claim: The NY Fed rejects weaker debt collection as the explanation for longer charge-off reporting, noting that recovery rates reported by the CFPB have only changed slightly, and instead points to changed lender reporting practices uncorrelated with debt performance.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Rules out the bearish interpretation (falling recoveries) and undercuts a distressed-consumer thesis for debt buyers and collection agencies; the change is administrative.

insights.claim: New delinquencies accelerated through the post-pandemic period, pushing stock and flow rates up together, but the pace of new delinquencies stabilized in early 2024 while the stock kept rising as charged-off debts accumulated.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Dates the regime break precisely — early 2024 — so any post-2024 divergence between the two series should be discounted as reporting drift, not new stress.

insights.claim: The NY Fed's bottom-line read on the consumer is that the pace of credit card delinquency is elevated but has been largely stable since 2024 — a two-sided message rather than an all-clear.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Elevated-but-flat supports carry in consumer credit rather than either a distress short or a recovery long; the risk is a break in the flow series, not the stock series.

insights.claim: The NY Fed defends the stock delinquency rate as still useful for gauging how much debt is owed to lenders and how much of it is delinquent, framing the two series as answering different questions rather than one being wrong.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Use stock for total household debt-burden and financial-inclusion questions, flow for cyclical timing — mixing them is the analytical error that produced the false alarm.
